title: cafaye trace signal
description: What a cafaye span is permitted to carry. The per-signal attribute allowlist for traces, and the shape of a span record that exports it. Three rules are encoded here rather than described in a README, because a rule that is not in schemas/ is not a cafaye rule (AGENTS.md): span names follow span-naming.schema.json, the attribute set is closed with additionalProperties: false so an attribute nobody thought about is a failure rather than a silent export, and no allowlisted name contains a word that names content. That last one is muse's canary promoted to a spec-level assertion — muse/tests/test_trace_propagation.py asserts the same property of muse's ALLOWED_SPAN_ATTRIBUTES end to end through a real request, and a real leak arrives as a well-meaning `muse.prompt` added in six months, not as an attacker. `error.message` is deliberately absent: a provider's content-policy rejection quotes the offending content back, so the message is a prompt by another route. `error.type` is the grouping key, and its vocabulary is a closed `enum` rather than a pattern — a pattern bounds the SHAPE of the value and not the set of values, so `user_42_email_invalid` used to validate, and on the metric side that is `tenant_id` on a measurement wearing a different name. Three semconv rules the attribute description alone cannot enforce are constraints here instead: span status `error` obliges an error class, an error class obliges a failed status (so the class is present exactly when the span failed, which is what makes its absence the load-bearing not-an-error marker), and `otel.status_code` may not contradict `status.code`. Handled and retried errors are not recorded at all — `SHOULD NOT` in semconv, and enforced here as unrepresentable: no signal allowlists an attribute a service could use to say 'this attempt failed and I recovered'. **Stability, honestly:** `error.type` and the span status rules are Stable in the OTel semantic conventions, but the document that defines the cross-signal coupling, `recording-errors.md`, is **Development**. Where this schema encodes that coupling it is encoding something not yet frozen; see D18. See docs/observability.md.

allOf.title: status error obliges an error class
allOf.description: `status.code: "error"` is a claim, and a claim has to be classifiable. core-04 stated this in a description and nowhere else — with the attribute deleted, span.muse.json still validated — so it is a constraint now. The inverse is the same rule read from the other side: a span that records a class has claimed it failed, and the field of record for that claim is `status.code`. Together the two make the class present **if and only if** the span failed, which is what makes its ABSENCE the load-bearing 'not an error' marker rather than an omission: on a duration histogram the samples carrying the class are the errors and every other sample is a success, and a success that carried one would move the numerator and make the error rate a number nobody can trust.

allOf.title: an error class obliges a failed status
allOf.description: The other direction of the same biconditional, and the reason it is two rules rather than one. A span whose status is `unset` while it carries an error class is a span that two different queries read differently, and nothing reports the disagreement.

allOf.title: the status mirror may not overrule the status
allOf.description: `otel.status_code` exists so a log-indexed query can filter on it, and `status.code` is the field of record. The moment the mirror can disagree with the field, a query that reads the mirror answers a different question from the predicate the fleet-wide view uses — and nothing anywhere reports that they differ. This is not a fifth rule: it is what makes the obligation above mean anything, because a span with two statuses has no status to be obliged.

name.description: Byte-identical to the pattern in span-naming.schema.json, which tests/test_specs.py asserts. A span name the traces schema accepts and the naming schema does not is a name core contradicts itself about.

kind.description: The OpenTelemetry span kind. A property of the span, never part of its name — a name that encodes the kind is a name that has to change when the relationship does.

attributes.description: The span's attributes, drawn from the trace allowlist. `additionalProperties: false` inside the allowlist itself, so a span carrying an attribute core has never heard of is rejected at the collector and in a service's own contract test rather than exported and stored.

resource.description: Attributes attached once per process rather than per span — service identity, version, deployment, tenancy. They are exempt from the metric cardinality cap, which is why identity belongs here and not on a measurement. See metrics.schema.json. Note what is NOT here: a `service` field on the span itself. The emitting service is `service.name` on the resource, because it is the same for every span the process emits — and restating it as a span field would be the same one-fact-two-places duplication this spec forbids for tenant_id on a measurement.

status.description: The OpenTelemetry span status. `code` is an enum rather than a string so a status cannot be invented per service; a service with a status core does not know about is a dashboard that silently misses it.

code.description: The OTel status code, and the field of record for whether this span failed — `otel.status_code` is a mirror of it for log-indexed queries and may not contradict it. `error` is a claim, and it obliges the span to carry `error.type`; that obligation is an `allOf` on this file's root, not this sentence.

message.description: A short static string for a human, such as `provider auth rejected`. Never an exception message, never a stack trace, never anything a caller or a vendor supplied: see the redaction boundary in redaction.schema.json.

links.description: Links to causally related spans, for the case a parent-child edge cannot express (a batch job whose items share no span). Bounded at 16, which is the OTel default link limit — an unbounded link list is a span whose size is a function of its data.

spanName.description: Byte-identical to `$defs/spanName` in span-naming.schema.json. Duplicated rather than `$ref`d because a service's SDK setup reads this file alone; a cross-file ref would make the file un-loadable without a resolver, and core's whole premise is that a service compiles against these files by path.

tracesAttributes.description: The complete set of attribute names a cafaye span may carry. Anything not listed is not emitted — default-deny, so an attribute added in a hurry is dropped rather than shipped. The dotted OpenTelemetry semantic-convention names are used for facts the ecosystem already has a name for, so a span exported to a backend nobody at cafaye has heard of is still readable. Each entry's `description` says what the attribute is a fact ABOUT, because the test that keeps content out is a test about names.

http.request.method.description: The HTTP method. Bounded by the enum, which is what makes it a legal measurement attribute too.

http.response.status_code.description: The response status. Bounded to 500 values. Note the metrics signal carries the *class* rather than the code — see metrics.schema.json.

http.route.description: The ROUTE TEMPLATE (`/v1/users/{id}`), never the concrete path. This is the distinction the whole attribute rule turns on: a template has one value per endpoint, a concrete path has one per request. `url.path` and `url.full` are not on the list for that reason, and neither is any query string — a query string is caller text by another name.

db.system.description: The database product. Four values; this is what a bounded dimension looks like.

db.operation.description: The database operation. A closed vocabulary of verbs rather than the statement text, which is caller-influenced and would be a leak on the SQL-injection path.

messaging.system.description: The transport. `postgres-outbox` is the fleet default (PLAN.md §7b: drain your own outbox, do not add a broker), so a span that crosses a service boundary says so by name.

messaging.operation.description: What the span did to the message. The delivery attempt count belongs here as a bounded integer, never the message body.

otel.status_code.description: The OTel status, mirrored as an attribute so a log-indexed query can filter on it. The span's own `status.code` is the field of record.

error.type.description: The error CLASS — a grouping key, and the reason there is one place to see all errors rather than a wall of ungrouped text (PLAN.md §7b). **Closed vocabulary, not a shape.** A `pattern` here would constrain the value's shape and say nothing about the set of values, so `user_42_email_invalid` would validate — snake_case, twenty-two characters, and one series per value, which on the metric side is `tenant_id` on a measurement wearing a different name. Byte-identical on all three signals, because a class that means one thing on traces and another on metrics is three taxonomies wearing one name; `ProviderAuthError` in Python and `ErrProviderAuth` in Go are one failure in two spellings, and that is how 'one place to see all errors' becomes six places. The twelve classes and the fallback: see D18 for why each earns its place, and D14 for the call this implements. `pattern` and `maxLength` stay as the second line and cannot reject a value the `enum` accepts. `_OTHER` is the only member outside the snake_case shape and is the OTel well-known fallback, spelled as the ecosystem spells it (D19): it exists so instrumentation is NEVER FORCED TO INVENT A CLASS, because a closed enum with no escape hatch gets widened under pressure the first time a real failure does not fit, and a widened enum is how `_OTHER` becomes a permanent value nobody reads. **An alert on `_OTHER` is an alert that this service has not classified its own errors** — real, actionable, and the argument for carrying it rather than omitting it. `error.message` is deliberately absent and never added: a provider's content-policy rejection quotes the offending content back, so the message is a prompt by another route. Handled and retried errors are not recorded here at all — `SHOULD NOT` in semconv, enforced on this signal as unrepresentable, since no allowlisted name can say 'this attempt failed and I recovered'. **Stability, honestly:** `error.type` and the span status rules are Stable, but the document defining the cross-signal coupling, `recording-errors.md`, is **Development**, and the obligations in this file's `allOf` are that coupling.

resource.description: Attributes attached once per process. Exempt from the 2000-combination metric cap and preserved on the overflow point, which is the correct home for identity — see metrics.schema.json for why that matters, and for why the same value on a measurement is the failure this whole spec exists to prevent.

service.namespace.description: The grouping this service belongs to — `cafaye` for every one of them. Stable in the OTel semantic conventions and the documented companion to `service.name`: it is what lets one collector group the fleet under a parent instead of showing seven unrelated services. muse sets it by hand (`src/muse/telemetry.py:390`) and is the only publisher that does, which is why it was missing here and why the list being closed cost a real span a validation it should have passed.

telemetry.sdk.name.description: Which SDK built this process's spans — `opentelemetry` in every language here. Stable semconv, and **not** an optional embellishment: billing sets it by hand at `lib/kit/telemetry.rb:183`, and the Python SDK's `Resource.create/1` merges it from its own default resource whether or not the caller asked. A service cannot suppress it without opting out of the SDK's defaults, so a resource allowlist without it does not describe a span — it describes the publishers whose resource is built without one, which is identity (Go's schemaless `resource.NewWithAttributes`) and courier (its own resource map).

telemetry.sdk.language.description: The implementation language, from the same two places as `telemetry.sdk.name`, and load-bearing for the same reason: a span that says which runtime produced it is what tells an operator that a fleet with four languages has four resource shapes. identity and courier report none of these three, for the reasons named beside `telemetry.sdk.name`.

telemetry.sdk.version.description: The SDK's own version — the fact that distinguishes two spans this spec cannot otherwise tell apart, since both satisfy every constraint above. Bounded to one value per process, like every other resource attribute, which is why it belongs here rather than on a measurement.

tenant_id.description: The tenant, here and never on a measurement. Unbounded as a dimension, exempt as a resource.

account_id.description: The account, same reasoning as tenant_id.
